newsitem.title: ITALY: FEATURE - Euro-friendly Italy fumbles EU-funds.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Euro-friendly Italy fumbles EU-funds.

text.p: Business leaders say it is a case of gross local bureaucratic bungling, the local regions say it is the problem of a bungling central bureaucracy.
Either way, impoverished southern Italy risks losing a fortune through its inability to tap huge pools of regional funds specially set up to boost development in the area.
Brussels has put aside some 30 trillion lire ($17.5 billion) for Italy's south for 1994-1999, while the central government in Rome has promised to match that amount when it is awarded.
All the regions have to do is find feasible projects.

But by the end of March, southern areas such as Sicily and Campania had spent less than 10 percent of the cash earmarked for them, leading the European Commission to warn that unless they get their act together, the money will go elsewhere.
Antonio Rastrelli, president of the Campania region which is centred in the bustling city of Naples, believes such threats are unfair, saying Brussels had no idea of the problem his officials faced.
"There are a jungle of laws out there we have to satisfy. It is a legislative hell," he told Reuters.
"In Italy there are 120,000 laws, in Germany 7,000 and in France 6,500. How is a poor person in the regions expected to navigate their way through 120,000 laws?" he said.

But one of Italy's two European Commissioners, Emma Bonino, argues that despite the fact Italy is one of the most fervant supporters of the European Union it has still has much to learn about the workings of the 15-nation bloc.
"Italian bureaucracy is without doubt the most ignorant when it comes to European administrative rights," she said in a newspaper interview.
SPAIN, PORTUGAL AND OTHERS PUT ITALY TO SHAME

Spain and Portugal have already used up almost all their allocated funds, some two years ahead of schedule, while Ireland and Greece are also proving much more nimble in their dealings with the EU than leaden-footed Italy.
With unemployment in southern Italy running at 22.5 percent against a national average of 12.5 percent, and its infrastructure notoriously haphazard, the regions can ill-afford to lose the EU money.
Yet businesses across the south accuse local authorities of doing little or nothing to help them make fund applications.

Many regions offer no technical assistance to guide firms through a minefield of regulations, while in Campania, fund-seekers are given a 38-page application dossier which applicants would need a law degree to understand.
"The only way to get anything done is to go into the offices with a pistol in your hand," said Maria Ceci, who has applied for money to refurbish her restaurant in the Calabria region.
The southern head of industrialists' group Confindustria, Antonio D'Amato, believes central government must move in immediately and take over the running of the funds.
"A fortune is going up in smoke here...there is no time to lose," he said.
Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi has already warned that unless regions raise the total of money spent to 38 percent by December, the government will take over the accounts.

The regions counter that they are working as fast as possible and accuse Ciampi of wanting to get his hands on regional money to help improve national accounts in the run up to the launch of the planned single European currency.
"Ciampi is trying to pull off an accounting trick. He wants regional money to help solidify accounts, but he is not going to touch a lira of it," Rastrelli said.
FEAR OF CORRUPTION HANGS OVER SOUTHERN ITALY
Calabria's regional president, Giuseppe Nistico, argues that it is not just suffocating local red tape causing delays.
"Bureaucracy isn't just our problem, Brussels is also very slow. At times for a small modification for a project you have to wait six months for the approval," he said.
Some officials in Campania believe that Brussels is over zealous with anything coming out of southern Italy.

"When they see the word Naples or Palermo on a request, they immediately think of organised crime and the Mafia. This makes them much more rigorous with their checks," said one local civil servant, who declined to be named.
But judging by the statistics, Brussels is wise to be wary of Italian fund allocations.
Although Italy is bottom of the class for use of EU funds it nonetheless has the highest level of fund fraud.

In 1996, Brussels uncovered fraud in the use of structural and agricultural funds in Italy to the tune of 147.9 million ecu ($165 million). Fraud from the second worst offender, Germany, totalled a mere 40.4 million ecu.
Commissioner Bonino believes that despite a recent campaign against corruption in Italy, the regions are still used to the old-fashioned way of doing business.

"Italy's public administration doesn't want to get used to European procedures...instead it prefers its public gravy train, blank checks, projects whose costs explode while the work is still going on," she said.
Despite the avalanche of criticism, the south swears it will reach the 38 percent spending threshold set by Ciampi for the end of 1997 and use up all the cash by the year 2000.
"I have a clear conscience, we are on course and will spend all the money on offer," Rastrelli said.
Brussels is sceptical. "It is clear that the spending target fixed by the (Italian) Treasury won't be met," Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn was quoted as saying in early July.
And the EU Commissioner for the regions, Monika Wulf-Mathies, came to Italy in person at the start of the month to deliver a stern warning.
"By 1998 at the latest there will have to be reallocation of funds which have not been used," she said.
($1 = 1,711 lire) ($ = 0.896 European Currency Unit ECUs)
